title: What I Learned from Studying in the UK
paragraphs: I did hospital clerkships for three months at the University of Warwick in the UK. It was my first long stay abroad, my first time living away from my parents, in an unfamiliar place among unfamiliar people. I went on this study abroad with anxiety, but although I worried every day, I was able to absorb a great deal, and it was a valuable experience.

During the three months of clerkships, I observed a total of five departments: nephrology, A&E (emergency), neurology, palliative care and oncology, and GP (community general practice). Most of the clerkships were done at University Hospital Coventry, which corresponds to a university hospital, the A&E at Warwick Hospital, and the GP at Woodside Medical Centre. The content of the clerkships in the UK was broadly similar to the Japanese polyclinic clerkships, and doing clerkships together with local students was a very enjoyable experience.

One of my goals for studying abroad was to learn about ways of practising medicine and being a doctor that differ from Japan, including the social-system background. I had researched the UK healthcare system in advance, but once I was in the actual setting, the bewilderment was greater than I had imagined. I would like to describe what I felt from comparing the UK and Japan.

First, I will introduce the UK healthcare system. The UK national healthcare service is called the National Health Service (NHS). Not only UK citizens but also immigrants and international students who hold a valid visa for a certain period of stay in the UK can use this service, and all medical costs are free. Eligible people register with a GP (General Practitioner), who corresponds to a family doctor, and except in emergencies they make an appointment with this GP before being seen. This GP is somewhat different from the image of a private practitioner in Japan, and is run by several doctors who have received specialist training. They do not have testing equipment such as X-ray machines, and examine patients on the basis of the history, physical examination and test data from outsourced tests. Even if a patient wishes to be seen, it may take two to three days to get an appointment. When the GP judges that more specialised treatment is needed, the patient is referred to an advanced medical institution such as a university hospital. The GP is the foundation of the UK healthcare system.

General practice has also attracted attention in Japan recently, and I especially looked forward to the GP clerkship during my study abroad. In the clerkship I observed consultations and home visits. Patients with various diseases come to the outpatient clinic. For patients with certain diseases, a system has been introduced in which the individual GP's pay is increased if they provide education such as lifestyle guidance and keep a record of it as data, which showed me that the country also puts emphasis on disease prevention. In addition, participation in weekly study sessions is mandatory, and they also work on updating their medical knowledge. However, when I observed outpatient clinics at the university hospital, I could not think that all GPs were functioning adequately. Most of the referred patients had mild conditions, and only a few truly needed specialised treatment. A doctor at the university hospital lamented that, as the knowledge required of GPs grows with medical advances, the number of doctors who cannot keep up with it is increasing. Even in the UK, which has long maintained the GP system, there are challenges in maintaining the quality of all-round doctors as medicine becomes more specialised. In my own future career too, after the two years of initial training, I will continue to study specialised knowledge, and I felt that how to maintain general competence as a doctor in the process is a big problem.

While having the GP system, the UK was also pushing forward the specialisation of allied health professionals. One example is the specialist nurse. There are specialist nurses for each disease, such as chronic kidney disease, Parkinson's disease and asthma, who make home visits, give telephone advice and run their own outpatient clinics, playing an intermediate role between the GP and advanced medical institutions. In every department, MDT (multidisciplinary team) meetings, where doctors, nurses and the other staff involved gather, were held frequently, and each profession evaluated the patient from its own viewpoint and shared information. I was very surprised at first that treatment that is considered a doctor's job in Japan is done by other allied health professionals (for example, some specialist nurses have trained and can prescribe drugs). It made me think again about what role a doctor should fulfil and what only doctors can do. However, even if a certain medical procedure can be done by both doctors and allied health professionals, which one is preferred may be up to the patient. Safety being ensured is of course a given condition, but I also felt that this might lead to treatment that better matches patients' feelings and convenience. Doctor shortages are said to be a problem in the UK too, but nursing stations and rehabilitation stations have been set up in the community, and allied health professionals can be said to play an important role in home care and visiting services. This is also effective as support for patients and their families who wish to live at home. There was much to learn in order to improve the situation in Japan, where nursing and care place a great burden on patients' families.

Another important element of the UK healthcare system is the existence of charity organisations. These organisations are run by donations, and I was very much helped in my clerkships by the staff of Macmillan, which supports cancer patients, and of Myton Hospice, which supports palliative and end-of-life care. In UK healthcare too, rising medical costs are a very big problem. In that situation, the existence of such organisations is indispensable for maintaining high-quality, attentive medical services. The act of donating was deeply rooted in everyday life in the UK. Walking around town, there were many recycling shops run by such charity organisations. The area where I stayed on this study abroad was, if anything, a poor area, but people seemed to donate as a matter of course within their own standard of living.

I learned a great deal from this study abroad experience, and unfortunately I cannot write everything here, but, both the enjoyable and the hard, I encountered many things I could never have experienced in Japan. I would like to take this opportunity to thank Dr. 粕谷 of the International Exchange Office, who gave me this valuable opportunity, everyone in the Student Affairs Office, the people who looked after me locally, the seniors who gave me advice, my classmates who supported me, and my family who sent me off. Thank you very much.
